newsitem.title: NORWAY: Norway needs tight fiscal stance - Central Bank. [CORRECTED 17:05 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Norway needs tight fiscal stance - Central Bank. [CORRECTED 17:05 GMT]

text.p: Norway's Central Bank chief Kjell Storvik on Wednesday called for a restrictive fiscal policy and wage moderation in 1997 to keep the country's strong economy under control.
In its third quarterly inflation report, the bank left its projections for inflation unchanged at 1.25 percent for 1996 and 2.5 percent in 1997.
But it said the rate of inflation may briefly rise to three percent at the end of 1996 due to a steep increase in electricity prices.

"Growth in the Norwegian economy is now considerably stronger than among our European trading partners, which makes it more demanding than otherwise to maintain price and wage inflation on a par with our trading partners," Storvik said.

"The risk of further pressures in the economy next year underlines the need for a tight fiscal policy stance in 1997, which is at least in line with the tightening originally called for in the budget of 1996."

Higher than expected wage growth forced the bank to upgrade in the second quarter its inflation forecast for the year to 2.5 percent from two percent (corrects to add dropped word "forecast"), and in the latest report Storvik said a tight fiscal stance in 1997 was central to help the bank maintain a stable exchange rate, the centrepiece of central bank policy.
"We want fiscal policy in the budget to be tight enough to deliver a stable exchange rate," Storvik told a news conference.
Analysts said the statement was a thinly veiled threat to the government, which is due to present the proposed 1997 budget to parliament on October 4.

"This is a sharpening of attitude. He (Storvik) is saying that if there's an expansionary budget then the Central Bank won't be there to bail the out the system or to stabilise inflation," said a chief analyst.
"He won't use monetary policy until the market has lost confidence in the crown. So he's asking for the market to react first and washing his hands of fiscal policy."
Norway suffered a wave of strikes in the spring as industrial unions used the strength of the economy as an argument for higher pay.
In the inflation report, the central bank upgraded estimates for wage growth next year to five percent from second-quarter forecasts of 4.75 percent, while maintaining 1996 growth at 4.25 percent.
Strong expansion in the economy had led to a tighter labour market despite employment rising faster than anticipated, it said.

In the first six months employment rose by 65,000 compared with the same period a year ago. However the decline in unemployment was smaller than the rise in the number of jobs would imply due to a larger participation in the workforce by women and youths.
Forecasts for unemployment were unchanged at 4.25 percent in 1996, edging down to four percent by the end of 1997.

"We are worried about developments in the labour market and that the tighter market will lead to higher inflation next year. I think there's a real risk inflation will pick up over the next 12 to 18 months," another Oslo-based analyst said.
The bank left unchanged projections for mainland gross domestic product at 3.25 percent in 1996 and 2.5 percent in 1997.
